blocks.body: The **Toffoli gate** (also called CCX or CCNOT) is a three-qubit gate with **two controls** and **one target**. The target is flipped only when **both** controls are |1⟩. This makes it a quantum version of the classical AND gate — and proves that quantum computers can do everything classical computers can.
Named after Tommaso Toffoli, who introduced it in 1980. The Toffoli gate is reversible (unitary), unlike classical AND, which is irreversible (you can't recover the inputs from the output).
The Toffoli gate maps |a, b, c⟩ → |a, b, c ⊕ (a·b)⟩. In other words, the target flips when both controls are 1:
If the target qubit starts as |0⟩, the Toffoli gate computes the AND of the two controls: |a, b, 0⟩ → |a, b, a·b⟩. Let's verify with both controls set to |1⟩:
Now with only one control set to |1⟩ — the target stays |0⟩:

The Toffoli gate can simulate any classical logic circuit. Since AND and NOT are a universal classical gate set, and Toffoli computes AND (with NOT available via X), quantum computers are **at least as powerful** as classical computers.

This is a key theoretical result: quantum computing is strictly more powerful than classical computing (assuming BQP ≠ BPP), because quantum computers can do everything classical ones can plus quantum operations like superposition and entanglement.
When the controls are in superposition, the Toffoli gate creates entanglement across all three qubits:

blocks.body: **Key takeaway:** The Toffoli gate flips the target when both controls are |1⟩ — a reversible AND gate. It proves quantum computers are at least as powerful as classical ones. Combined with H, it enables quantum computation on classical logic.
